course_name_original: ECONOMIA GENERAL Y DE LA EMPRESA

learning_outcomes.text: Apply acquired knowledge to identify, formulate, and solve problems in broad contexts, being capable of integrating them by working in multidisciplinary teams.
Understand the impact of engineering on the environment, the sustainable development of society, and the importance of working in a professional and responsible environment.
Communicate knowledge and conclusions, both orally and in writing, to specialized and non-specialized audiences clearly and unambiguously.
Possess learning skills that allow for lifelong learning for adequate professional development.
Adequate knowledge of the concept of business, its institutional and legal framework. Business organization and management.
Know and apply basic science and technology knowledge to the practice of Industrial Engineering.
Organization and planning of projects and human teams. Teamwork and leadership capacity.
Knowledge and capabilities to understand the functioning of the economy in general and that of the company in particular.

syllabus_topics: 1.1.1. Concept of Economy: what, how, for whom it is produced.
1.1.2. Orthodox versus heterodox approach in economics.
1.1.2.1. Efficiency, production possibility frontier, externalities, market failures.
1.1.3. Basic principles in Economics according to Mankiw and other authors.
1.1.5. Economy, as a social and political science.
1.1.5.1. Human behavior sciences and the current complexity of the economy.
1.2.1.1. Production function, cost function and supply function of the firm.
1.2.2.1. Budget line and consumer preferences. Demand function.
1.3.1.1. Macro-magnitudes, indicators: GDP, inflation, unemployment, debt, deficit, balance of payments.
1.3.1.1.1. Added Value, Production and GDP; Savings and Disposable Income. Financing capacity of an economy.
1.3.1.2.1. The problem of unemployment: job search, minimum wage and efficiency wages.
1.3.2. Brief presentation of macroeconomic policies: fiscal, monetary, exchange rate, and supply-side.
1.4.1. Labor market, public sector, financial sector, productive structure and growth.
1.5.1. Structure of Balance of Payments and financing capacity of an economy.
2.1. THE COMPANY AS A SYSTEM AND ITS INSTITUTIONAL AND LEGAL FRAMEWORK.
2.1.1.1. Strategic analysis of the company's environment: general and specific (sector).
2.1.1.1.1. Analysis of the five forces of a sector.
2.1.2. The company as an institutional, open system and its objectives.
2.1.2.1. Organization theory, agency theory, transaction cost theory, and institutions.
2.1.2.2. Standardization of institutional and productive quality in a global environment.
2.1.3.1. Public law, private law, civil law, patrimonial law and commercial law.
2.1.3.2. Company and entrepreneur. Types of companies.
2.1.3.2.1. Economic dimension of the entrepreneur, company size.
2.1.3.3. Commercial contracting: contract, securities and book-entry shares.
2.2.1.1. Organization theories: classical, human relations, contingency approach, information sciences and knowledge management.
2.2.1.3. Management functions: planning, organizing, executing, controlling, and safety management.
2.2.1.3.1. Planning: definition of objectives and strategies (business, functional and growth).
2.2.1.3.1.1. Sustainability, strategy, and ESG criteria (environmental, social and governance).
2.2.1.3.2. Organization: organizational design variables and types of organizational structures.
2.2.1.3.3.1. Organizational learning, Artificial Intelligence and intellectual capital.
2.2.2.4. General Accounting Plan: framework, principles and standards.
2.3.1.1. Strategic decisions: product design, process, location and production plant.
2.3.1.2. Operational decisions: operational planning and control, inventory management, quality and its costs.
2.3.2.1.1. Concepts: need, desire, value, product, value, cost, satisfaction and exchange.
2.3.2.2. Operational marketing: product, price, communication and distribution decisions.
2.4.1.1.1. Investment decision, costs, cash flows and profits.
2.4.1.1.3.1. Investment cycle, average maturation period, working capital and cash flow.
2.4.1.1.3.2. Financial cycle, weighted average cost of capital, financial leverage and dividend policy.
2.4.1.3.1. Internal financing: Partner contributions and self-financing.
2.4.1.3.2. External financing: long and short term. Types.
assessment_rules: For progressive evaluation, two written controls must be passed independently, one for each part of the course, with a minimum of 4 out of 10 in each. Two group works are evaluated, each with a weight of 10%, totaling 20%. The course is passed when a final average of 5 is obtained. For evaluation solely by final exam, there is a global final exam consisting of 5 questions (theoretical-practical, problems, cases), each worth 2 points. For the extraordinary exam, there is a global final exam consisting of 5 questions (theoretical-practical, problems, cases), each worth 2 points. If a student who passed by progressive evaluation takes the global final exam in January, the grade from this global final exam will be the final grade.
